name: Language Models and Diagnosis
blurb: How medical language models compare with physicians.
title: Language Models and Diagnosis
answer: Medical language models now pass licensing exam style questions comfortably; Med-PaLM 2 scored about 86.5 percent on the MedQA dataset. Exam scores are not clinical performance, and studies of real diagnostic reasoning show mixed results that depend heavily on how clinicians use the tool.

reading.body:
Medical language models pass licensing-style exams comfortably, but exam scores are not clinical performance, and real diagnostic reasoning results are mixed.

The clearest number here is Med-PaLM 2 at about 86.5 percent on MedQA, reported by Google researchers in Nature Medicine in January 2025. MedQA is a licensing exam question set. A high score means the model retrieves and applies medical knowledge well under exam conditions, where the question is posed cleanly and one answer is correct. That is a knowledge test, not a measure of what happens when a patient arrives with an incomplete history and several conditions at once.

The research record around this page points the same direction. The papers listed cover generalist diagnosis assistance, interactive image-based diagnosis, triage and referral workflows, knowledge graphs for diagnosis prediction, and uncertainty calibration. Several are about workflow and calibration rather than raw accuracy. That is the tell: the open problem is not whether the model knows medicine, it is whether the model knows when it does not know, and whether the clinician using it can tell the difference.

What the data does not cover is deployment scale. There is one company named, one dated development, and no figures on how many care teams use these tools or what happened when they did. The finding that results depend heavily on how clinicians use the tool is stated but not quantified here. So the honest reading is that capability on exams is established and clinical benefit is not, and the gap between them is a workflow and trust problem rather than a knowledge problem.
